dimensions.name: Understanding the pipeline, data, and loading contract

evidence.note: Solid initial environment probing: listed workspace, cat'd the template, inspected data dir and tokenizer, checked GPU (H100), PyTorch version, sentencepiece, pip list, and measured data shard format (uint16, 137M train tokens, 589K val, vocab 8192). Grounds design in measured facts — matches the probing described in anchors 5/8.

Deliberately verified part of the loading contract: ran save/load round-trips, checked reloaded loss (9.1759 vs 9.1773) and explicitly confirmed the model(input_ids, target_ids) loss == F.cross_entropy contract passes exactly. This is genuine contract reverse-engineering (anchor 8 territory).

Tested compression schemes (zlib vs lzma vs checking zstd/brotli availability) and later diagnosed torch.save pickle overhead (~3.3MB), switching to raw-binary serialization — real byte accounting incl. compression. But serialization bugs (flat tensors losing shape @113, GPU .numpy() crash @128) were discovered reactively during runs, not anticipated.

Only at step 84 did the agent measure bytes_per_token (~3.87) and realize its val_bpb computation was wrong (bits-per-token vs bits-per-byte), having earlier believed the target was loss<0.681. This core metric understanding was flawed through ~3 training runs and corrected late — a significant orientation gap.

Parameter/size budget was learned reactively through repeated overflow failures (54M→35M→30M→33M→36M→33M→29M) rather than derived up front. The agent understood int8+compression drives the budget but never produced a clean first-principles bytes-per-param picture before committing compute.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it probed the environment (GPU, data volume, tokenizer, vocab), confirmed the .bin format, and additionally verified the forward/loss cross_entropy contract, dequant round-trips, and byte accounting including compression — elements of anchor 8. However, it falls well short of 8/10 because two critical facets of understanding were reactive rather than deliberate: the bpb metric was computed wrong until step 84 (after multiple wasted runs), and the param/size budget was discovered through repeated overflow failures rather than derived up front. This mix of strong contract/environment probing but late, empirically-corrected understanding of the metric and size budget places it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Staging the build: pipeline → budget → scale → quantize → verify

evidence.note: Opened with a distinct environment/understanding stage (workspace, data format, tokenizer, GPU/PyTorch, package availability) before writing any training code — a deliberate first milestone.

Before the first long run, ran concrete pre-launch gates: syntax check, model creation, save/load round-trip, cross_entropy-contract check (step 10), and compressed checkpoint size vs 32MB. Repeatedly resized (54M→32.5M→30M) until compressed size fit under budget — an explicit size-budget done-check preceding training.

The size gate was NOT robustly front-loaded: the agent repeatedly LAUNCHED long training then killed runs upon discovering the checkpoint grew past 32MB during training (trained weights compress worse than init). Size overflow was rediscovered mid-run several times, wasting compute — the high-risk invalidator was not retired before the expensive step.

torch.compile C-compiler crash and the val_bpb metric miscalculation were both discovered at runtime rather than caught by a cheap pre-flight check, indicating reactive rather than fully risk-ordered gating.

Later milestone-driven adaptation: introduced raw-binary format and lzma to reclaim space, then sized a 19-layer/29.3M model with an explicit ~6.75MB margin (25.2MB init) so the size gate would survive training growth — a concrete, quantitative gate finally set before the final run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly staged the work: understand environment → write script → verify param count/compressed size/save-load/cross_entropy contract → launch → measure local val_bpb → scale/resize, with concrete pre-launch success criteria (fits 32MB with margin, round-trip loads, contract holds). That is more than anchor 5's rough criteria, matching the concrete-gate spirit of anchor 8. But it falls short of 8/10 because the ordering was not risk-optimal: the size-overflow failure mode was rediscovered deep inside multiple expensive runs rather than retired up front, and crashes/metric bugs surfaced at runtime — so the milestones read as an implicit, partly-reactive sequence rather than a front-loaded, quantitatively-gated hierarchy. This lands at 6.

dimensions.name: Independently verifying loadability, contract, size, and bpb

evidence.note: Loaded its own saved checkpoint back, checked compressed size, and explicitly confirmed the model(ids,targets) loss equals F.cross_entropy ('check passes exactly'); noted reload loss drift from int8 quantization — round-trip fidelity awareness.
Discovered local val_bpb was bits-per-token not bits-per-byte, computed bytes/token≈3.87, and corrected the target to match how the grader computes bpb — aligning the proxy metric.
Caught and re-tested multiple real load/serialization bugs: shape-loss in raw binary, GPU .numpy() crash, backward-compat dequantize — genuine round-trip verification catching breakage.
Repeatedly verified compressed checkpoint size against the 32MB cap throughout, using it to trigger architecture downsizing.

Final 'verification' was superficial (import test that functions are defined); no fresh-process load via exact load_model_for_verification signature nor logits-shape/position checks. Submitted with val_bpb=1.026 (above 0.983), misusing the ~0.05 agreement tolerance as a pass margin rather than gating submission on a passing check.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it loaded checkpoints back through save/load, confirmed ≤32MB, confirmed the loss==cross_entropy contract, corrected its bpb metric to mirror the grader, verified int8 dequant round-trip fidelity, and caught several real serialization bugs. But it falls short of 8: verification was piecemeal and reactive rather than a consolidated fresh-process harness testing the exact load_model_for_verification signature, logits shape, and position dependence, and it never gated submission on a passing check — instead marking complete with val_bpb above target while misinterpreting the proxy-gap tolerance as slack. This places it at a 6, between the solid-basics anchor (5) and the standalone-harness anchor (8).

dimensions.name: Tracking bpb trajectory and detecting plateaus/divergence

evidence.note: Recognized its val_bpb formula was wrong (bits/token vs bits/byte), computed bytes_per_token≈3.87, and recalibrated the target to val_loss<2.635 — a genuine monitoring calibration correction that made all subsequent tracking accurate.

Maintained a quantitative extrapolated view: tracked val_loss curve (3.30→2.95→2.84→2.79), quantified diminishing improvement per 2500 steps, estimated steps-to-target, and simultaneously extrapolated checkpoint-size growth against the 32MB limit.
Detected plateau in the resume run (val_loss stuck ~2.70, improvement near-zero per 1000 steps) and killed it rather than waiting to the end — acting on the trajectory read.
Read that the 22-layer run's size would breach 32MB before hitting target given the loss/size rates, killed it, and switched to a smaller 19-layer model for margin.
Continued projecting time-to-target vs wall-clock (val 2.818→2.765, rate slowing to ~0.02/2500), correctly noting diminishing returns and remaining gap.

Final lapse: marked task complete with val_bpb=1.026 (target 0.983) on a plateauing run, misreading the grader's 0.05 proxy-agreement tolerance as a target margin — an unreliable final 'will it pass' judgment.

dimensions.reasoning: Across the whole horizon the agent periodically evaluated val_bpb against 0.983, tracked the curve's diminishing returns quantitatively, projected time-to-target against remaining budget, and acted on those reads by killing plateaued/oversized runs early — squarely matching the level-8 anchor and reaching into level-10 territory. It falls short of 10 because its final projection was unreliable: it declared success on a clearly plateauing run still ~0.05 bpb above target, conflating proxy-agreement tolerance with target margin. That single misread of 'will this pass' keeps it at a strong 8 rather than a clean 9-10.

dimensions.name: Revising architecture/hyperparameters/quantization when reality diverges

evidence.note: First size overflow (54M→50MB): diagnosed model too large, iteratively downsized to ~32M and re-verified compressed size before proceeding — reasoned change, not a blind retry.

Diagnosed that trained weights compress worse than init causing 32.55MB overflow; empirically tested lzma/zstd/brotli and adopted lzma for ~3MB gain — evidence-driven attack on the actual (compression) bottleneck.
Computed bytes_per_token (~3.87) to correct its misunderstanding of the bpb target, re-deriving the true val_loss threshold — a genuine diagnostic correction mid-run.
Diagnosed torch.save pickle overhead (~3.3MB) and switched to raw binary serialization to buy size margin — targeted the real quantization/serialization cost, a level-8-style bottleneck fix.
Diagnosed resume plateau as LR-driven and restarted with full schedule; later reduced 33M→19-layer 29M to guarantee a 6.75MB margin against training-induced growth — rebalancing params vs budget.

Countervailing thrash: premature kill at step 750, overwrote its best checkpoint by restarting from scratch, and repeated serialization bugs — re-running the same convergence curve rather than converging efficiently.
Submitted at val_bpb ~1.03 (target 0.983), rationalizing 'within tolerance' — never actually reached target, showing the corrections did not converge to a passing config.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's course-corrections were consistently evidence-driven and repeatedly hit the actual binding constraint — recognizing quantization/compression (zlib→lzma→raw-binary) was costing size and rebalancing params vs steps against the 32MB budget — which is squarely the level-8 anchor's behavior. However, it did not converge efficiently: it re-ran the same 3.30→2.95→2.84 convergence curve across many restarts, killed runs prematurely, overwrote its best checkpoint, and ultimately submitted a still-above-target model, which is the 're-debugging in circles' the level-10 anchor excludes. That places it above the reasoned-single-fix level 5 but below the efficient systematic-isolation of 8-10, i.e., a 7.

dimensions.name: Allocating finite compute across exploration and the final run

evidence.note: Before the first long run, the only pre-launch checks were param-count and compressed-size tests; no cheap short training experiment was done to de-risk the recipe before committing to a full 12000-step run — exploration budget was not carved out.

Repeated pattern of launching full-length runs (12k/50k/40k steps) and killing them at steps 750-2000, almost always reacting to checkpoint-size overflow rather than a deliberate exploration-vs-final allocation; compute spent on aborted full runs instead of cheap probes.

Full 100k-step run from scratch; agent used early-checkpoint trajectory (3.30@2500→2.95@5000→2.84@7500) to extrapolate when target would be hit and sized to remaining wall-clock — genuine scaling intuition — but then killed the run at step 7500 for size, wasting the compute.

Final 19-layer run plateaued at val_bpb~1.03 (target 0.983); agent spent the last ~2 hours in repeated 'wait 30 minutes' loops with no reallocation, no reserve, and no cheap experiment to escape the plateau — budget was consumed without reaching target.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows more than ad-hoc awareness (anchor 3): it extrapolates early-checkpoint loss curves to the final configuration and sizes runs to remaining wall-clock via throughput, which is genuine scaling-informed reasoning. But it never runs the cheap small-scale de-risking experiments or keeps a reserve that anchor 5 requires — instead it repeatedly launches expensive full runs and kills them reactively, and it burns the final two hours idly waiting on a plateauing run. This chaotic, wasteful allocation lands between anchors 3 and 5, at 4.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML engineering task: train a language model on a WikiText BPE-8K corpus and submit a ≤32MB int8-quantized checkpoint that scores val_bpb < 0.983 on a held-out split. Difficulty comes from a joint constraint (fit under 32MB after quantization AND beat the bpb target), an exact and dual-path loading/forward/loss contract that silently fails if violated, iterative training under a noisy local proxy (val shard ≈±0.05 of grader), and finite compute. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily in understanding the template and contract, planning the parameter/size budget, building an independent verification harness, and monitoring/adapting training over many hours.

dimensions.name: Understanding the pipeline, data, and loading contract
dimensions.description: Reading the template, tokenizer, .bin data format, int8 quantization scheme, bpb metric, and the exact verification/loading contract before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task hides two traps: an exact dual-path load/forward/loss contract (a subtle mismatch scores zero regardless of model quality) and a hard byte budget. Acting before understanding these wastes an entire training run.

anchors.0: Starts editing/training with no inspection of the template, data shards, tokenizer, or loading contract.
anchors.3: Skims the template and runs it; unaware of the forward(input_ids, target_ids) loss requirement, the two load paths, or how bpb is computed.
anchors.5: Reads the template and the contract, confirms data shard format and tokenizer/vocab size, and understands that int8 + size drive a parameter budget before committing to an architecture.
anchors.8: Deliberately reverse-engineers the full contract (both load paths, logits-depend-on-position, loss==cross_entropy tolerance, int8 dequant round-trip, exact byte accounting incl. compression) and probes the environment (GPU, data volume, tokenizer) so the design is grounded in measured facts, not assumptions.
anchors.10: Above, plus derives a quantitative param/size/bpb picture from first principles (bytes-per-param under int8+compression, rough capacity-vs-bpb intuition), and pins down every ambiguity in the contract with a tiny probe before investing compute — leaving no silent-failure mode unexamined.

dimensions.name: Staging the build: pipeline → budget → scale → quantize → verify
dimensions.description: Breaking the work into ordered milestones (working end-to-end tiny run, size budget, local bpb measurement, scale-up, quantization, contract verification) each with an explicit done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The joint size/quality/contract constraint means a monolithic 'train a big model' push risks discovering at the end that it's oversized or unloadable. Ordered milestones de-risk the horizon.

anchors.0: One undifferentiated attempt: configure a model and train, with no intermediate checkpoints of progress.
anchors.3: Implicit stages in the agent's head but no explicit sub-goals or done-criteria; ordering is reactive.
anchors.5: Clear sequence: get a tiny model training and saving/loading first, establish the param budget, measure local val_bpb, then scale — with rough success criteria per stage.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with concrete gates (e.g. 'end-to-end quantized round-trip loads and scores locally before any long run'; 'param count fits 32MB with margin'), sequenced so that cheap high-risk checks (contract, size) precede expensive ones (long training).
anchors.10: Milestones are risk-ordered and quantitatively gated, explicitly front-loading the failure modes that would waste the most compute (contract conformance, size overflow, quant degradation) so a long final run is only launched once every cheap invalidator has been retired.

dimensions.name: Independently verifying loadability, contract, size, and bpb
dimensions.description: Designing checks beyond 'training loss went down': that the checkpoint loads via the specified path, forward/loss contract holds, file is ≤32MB, quantization round-trips, and local bpb mirrors the grader's computation.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader loads through a strict interface and enforces a hard byte cap; a great model that violates any of these scores zero. Verification is the single highest-leverage meta-work faculty here.

anchors.0: Trains and submits without ever loading its own checkpoint through the grader's interface or checking file size.
anchors.3: Checks training loss and maybe file size, but never exercises the actual load_model_for_verification / dequant path or confirms the loss==cross_entropy contract.
anchors.5: Loads the saved checkpoint back through the specified path, confirms it is ≤32MB, and computes local val_bpb the way the grader would; catches obvious breakage.
anchors.8: Builds a standalone verification harness that mimics the grader end-to-end (fresh-process load via the exact signature, logits-shape and position-dependence, scalar-loss equality within tolerance, int8 dequant fidelity, byte count) and treats passing it as the gate for submission.
anchors.10: Verification harness is comprehensive and adversarial: tests both load paths, quantify's quantization's bpb cost separately from the fp model, accounts for the ~0.05 proxy-vs-grader gap by targeting margin below 0.983, and re-runs after every material change so no regression reaches submission unnoticed.

dimensions.name: Tracking bpb trajectory and detecting plateaus/divergence
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of val_bpb vs the 0.983 target over training, and detecting overfitting, divergence, plateau, or wasted runs across the horizon.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Training is long and the only feedback is a noisy local proxy; without disciplined monitoring the agent burns compute on a run that will never reach target or silently overfits.

anchors.0: No periodic val evaluation; discovers final bpb only at the end (or never).
anchors.3: Occasionally glances at loss but no consistent val_bpb tracking against the target; can't say how far from passing.
anchors.5: Periodically evaluates val_bpb during training and compares to 0.983, noticing obvious plateaus or divergence.
anchors.8: Tracks the val_bpb trajectory against target with enough cadence to project whether the current run will pass, distinguishing real signal from proxy noise, and identifies stuck/plateaued runs early rather than at the end.
anchors.10: Maintains a quantitative, extrapolated view (curve shape, diminishing returns, time-to-target vs remaining budget) that reliably distinguishes 'keep training', 'this run won't make it', and 'overfitting' — and acts on that read before compute is wasted.

dimensions.name: Revising architecture/hyperparameters/quantization when reality diverges
dimensions.description: Changing the model size, training recipe, or quantization approach when a run overflows the budget, fails to converge, plateaus above target, or loses bpb to quantization.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First attempts rarely satisfy both the size cap and the bpb target; the ability to diagnose why and change course (rather than re-running the same losing configuration) determines whether the task is ever passed.

anchors.0: Repeats the same failing configuration, or ignores that the checkpoint is oversized / above target, and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks after a failure without diagnosing the cause; changes are not clearly informed by evidence.
anchors.5: When a run overflows size or misses the bpb target, diagnoses the likely cause and makes a reasoned change (smaller/larger model, longer training, different lr) before retrying.
anchors.8: Course-corrections are evidence-driven and target the actual bottleneck (e.g. recognizes quantization is costing bpb and adjusts scheme; rebalances params vs steps against the size budget) rather than thrashing across unrelated knobs.
anchors.10: Systematically isolates whether size, capacity, optimization, or quantization is the binding constraint and adapts the design accordingly, updating the plan/budget in light of what was learned — converging efficiently instead of re-debugging in circles.

dimensions.name: Allocating finite compute across exploration and the final run
dimensions.description: Deciding how much compute to spend on small-scale experiments vs the long final training run, informed by rough scaling intuition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Compute is finite and a full training run is expensive; spending it all on exploration or committing early to an unvalidated long run both fail. Deliberate allocation is a distinct planning faculty here.

anchors.0: No sense of budget; either endlessly tinkers at small scale or immediately commits everything to one untested long run.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware compute is limited but allocation is ad hoc.
anchors.5: Runs cheap small-scale experiments to de-risk choices before committing to a longer run, keeping some budget in reserve.
anchors.8: Explicitly allocates budget between exploration and the final run, using small runs to inform architecture/recipe and sizing the final run to fit remaining compute.
anchors.10: Uses scaling-informed reasoning (small-run signal extrapolated to the final configuration) to spend compute where it most improves bpb, avoiding both premature commitment and analysis paralysis, and adjusts allocation as results come in.
